OwnershipNFTs.sol has custom implementation of `safeTransferFrom()`. After _transfer it calls `_onTransferReceived()`, which has require statement at the end. 
Requirement checks if returned data from _to-`IERC721TokenReceiver(_to).onERC721Received()` is equal to `IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector`. 

for success execution returned data and internal selector won't be equal, but thats incorrect.

```solidity
    function _onTransferReceived(
        address _sender,
        address _from,
        address _to,
        uint256 _tokenId
    ) internal {
        // only call the callback if the receiver is a contract
        if (_to.code.length == 0) return;

        bytes4 data = IERC721TokenReceiver(_to).onERC721Received(
            _sender,
            _from,
            _tokenId,

            // this is empty byte data that can be optionally passed to
            // the contract we're confirming is able to receive NFTs
            ""
        );

            data != IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector,
            "bad nft transfer received data"

require statement on line 92-95 must be check if them are equal, but here we see opposite, so we can say that some non-EOA(e.x. safeWallet, gnosis) can't use `safeTransferFrom` function.

Change 93 line:

require(

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The current implementation of the `lib.rs` smart contract allows users to perform 2 stage swaps using `swap_2_exact_in_41203_F1_D()` function. The function calls several internal functions where the last ones are `swap_2_internal()` and `swap()` from the pool. The problem is that the `swap_2_internal()` only allows to specify `minOut` amount not taking into account price limit that's used in the pool `swap()` function for slippage protection. This leads to a situation where user will be subjected to MEV attacks and may not be able to perform the swap during a huge amount of time as `min_out` will be repeatedly < `amount_out`.

## Proof of Concept

Take a look at the current functionality of `swap_2_internal()`:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/seawater/src/lib.rs#L210-215
```
  let (amount_in, interim_usdc_out, final_tick_in) = pools.pools.setter(from).swap(
            true,
            amount,
            // swap with no price limit, since we use min_out instead
            tick_math::MIN_SQRT_RATIO + U256::one(),
        )?;

```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/seawater/src/lib.rs#L223-227

let (amount_out, interim_usdc_in, final_tick_out) = pools.pools.setter(to).swap(
            false,
            interim_usdc_out,
            tick_math::MAX_SQRT_RATIO - U256::one(),
        )?;

```

As you can see, both time `price_limit` value is set to maximum effectively meaning that there is no slippage. Therefore, users can be subjected to the MEV attacks and not being able to perform the swap successfully as the `min_out` will be repeatedly less than `amount_out`.

Manual review.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/seawater/src/lib.rs#L81


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The current implementation of the `SeawaterAMM` smart contract uses Diamond-like proxy pattern directing calls to the implementation contracts via delegatecall. It enables the users to call different functions from different features. The problem is that the contract initializes `EXECUTOR_FALLBACK_SLOT` and assigns the corresponding smart contract address of the Rust implementation but there is no currently such feature in the Rust code.

## Proof of Concept

`EXECUTOR_FALLBACK_SLOT` is assigned to the corresponding address in the internal `_setProxies()` function:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L568
```
StorageSlot.getAddressSlot(EXECUTOR_FALLBACK_SLOT).value = address(executorFallback);
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L30
```
bytes32 constant EXECUTOR_FALLBACK_SLOT = bytes32(uint256(keccak256("seawater.impl.fallback")) - 1);
```

As you can see from the next lines, the "fallback" feature is called in the `fallback()` function if no any other feature does not correspond to the `msg.data` sent to the contract:


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L520
```
        else directDelegate(_getExecutorFallback());
    }
```

`directDelegate` in its turn calls implementation address (in the terms of the protocol, it's "features" in the Rust code):


https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L129-132
```

 // call a function with the same name and calldata on another contract
    // this ends execution!
    // proxy implementation adapted from openzeppelin
    function directDelegate(address to) internal 

```

As the comment above points out, the proxy implementation is adapted from the OZ meaning `directDelegate` is similar to the `_delegate()` function from the `Proxy` contract that calls implementation.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/seawater/src/lib.rs#L81-89
```
#[cfg(not(any(
    feature = "swaps",
    feature = "swap_permit2",
    feature = "quotes",
    feature = "positions",
    feature = "update_positions",
    feature = "admin",
    feature = "migrations"
)))]

```

Manual review.

## Impact

The current functionality of `OwnershipNFTs` smart contract allows to make approvals of the NFT positions to other addresses. ## Proof of Concept

Here's the current `approve()` behavior:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L160-163
```
   /// @inheritdoc IERC721Metadata
    function approve(address _approved, uint256 _tokenId) external payable {
        _requireAuthorised(msg.sender, _tokenId);
        getApproved[_tokenId] = _approved;
    }
```

It calls `_requireAuthorised()` function as well as the functions for NFT transfer do for authorization purposes. But, in comparison with ERC-721 standard, it uses different implementation:

https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol#L415-417
```
// We do not use _isAuthorized because single-token approvals should not be able to call approve

            if (auth != address(0) && owner != auth && !isApprovedForAll(owner, auth)) {
                revert ERC721InvalidApprover(auth);
            }
```

As you can see, there are several deviations from the ERC-721 standard:


1. The function `requireAuthorized()` requires for the `from` address (that is a `msg.sender` who calls `approve()`) to be the owner while in the ERC-721 standard it's `auth` address.

2. It checks whether `msg.sender` is in the `getApproved` mapping for the given tokenID while in the ERC-721 standard it's only `isApprovedForAll()`.

3. `isApprovedForAll()` checks if the `isApprovedForAll[_from][msg.sender]` statement is true (where `_from` is always msg.sender) where in the implementation of the standard it checks for the `isApprovedForAll(owner, auth)` where `auth` can differ from the `owner`.

This makes the contract non ERC-721 compatible and leads to the users not being able to give approvals of their tokenIDs to other addresses as it's required

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Change the check for authorization inside of the `approve()` function to make it ERC-721 compatible.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L74-L97


# Vulnerability details


The `OwnershipNFTs` contract is designed to track ownership of positions in the `Seawater` contract. One of its functions, [`_onTransferReceived`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L74-L97), is responsible for ensuring that the recipient of an NFT can handle ERC721 tokens. This is done by calling the `onERC721Received` function on the recipient contract and checking its return value.

The ERC721 standard specifies that the `onERC721Received` function should return a specific selector (`0x150b7a02`) to confirm that the contract can handle the token. If the returned value does not match this selector, the transfer should be reverted.

However, the current implementation of `_onTransferReceived` contains a bug. The `require` statement incorrectly uses `!=` instead of `==`, which means it will revert if the returned data is equal to the expected selector. This is the opposite of the intended behavior. The function should revert if the returned data is **not** equal to the expected selector.

The relevant code is as follows:

```solidity
File: OwnershipNFTs.sol
74:     function _onTransferReceived(
75:         address _sender,
76:         address _from,
77:         address _to,
78:         uint256 _tokenId
79:     ) internal {
80:         // only call the callback if the receiver is a contract
81:         if (_to.code.length == 0) return;
82: 
83:         bytes4 data = IERC721TokenReceiver(_to).onERC721Received(
84:             _sender,
85:             _from,
86:             _tokenId,
87: 
88:             // this is empty byte data that can be optionally passed to
89:             // the contract we're confirming is able to receive NFTs
90:             ""
91:         );
92:         // @audit - This should be == instead of !=. It's currently rejecting valid transfers and allowing invalid ones.
93:         require(
94:             data != IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector,
95:             "bad nft transfer received data"
96:         );
97:     }

```

## Impact
This causes the contract to reject valid NFT transfers and allow invalid ones. This could lead to a situation where NFTs are transferred to contracts that cannot handle them, potentially resulting in the loss of NFTs. Conversely, valid transfers to compliant contracts will be incorrectly reverted, disrupting the intended functionality of the contract.

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice attempts to transfer an NFT to Bob's contract, which correctly implements `onERC721Received`.
2. The `_onTransferReceived` function is called, and Bob's contract returns the correct selector (`0x150b7a02`).
3. The `require` statement incorrectly reverts the transaction because it checks for `!=` instead of `==`.
4. The valid transfer is rejected, and Alice's NFT remains with her.

Conversely:
1. Alice attempts to transfer an NFT to Charlie's contract, which does not implement `onERC721Received`.
2. The `_onTransferReceived` function is called, and Charlie's contract returns an incorrect value.
3. The `require` statement does not revert the transaction because it checks for `!=` instead of `==`.
4. The invalid transfer is allowed, and the NFT is sent to a contract that cannot handle it.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `require` statement should be corrected to use `==` instead of `!=` to comply with the ERC721 standard. This ensures that the transfer is only accepted if the recipient contract correctly implements the `onERC721Received` function.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L125-L246


# Vulnerability details


The [`get_fee_growth_inside` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L125-L246) in the `StorageTicks` struct is responsible for calculating the fee growth inside a given tick range. This function is crucial for determining the fees accrued within a specific range of ticks, which is essential for liquidity providers in a decentralized exchange or automated market maker (AMM) protocol.

The function calculates the fee growth inside the range by subtracting the fee growth outside the range from the global fee growth. However, there is a logical error in how it handles the fee growth calculations when the current tick (`cur_tick`) is outside the given range (`lower_tick` to `upper_tick`). This can lead to incorrect fee growth calculations, potentially resulting in financial discrepancies for liquidity providers.

The issue arises in the following part of the code:

```rust
let (fee_growth_below_0, fee_growth_below_1) = if cur_tick >= lower_tick {
    (
        lower.fee_growth_outside_0.get(),
        lower.fee_growth_outside_1.get(),
    )
} else {
    (
        fee_growth_global_0
            .checked_sub(lower.fee_growth_outside_0.get())
            .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubTick)?,
        fee_growth_global_1
            .checked_sub(lower.fee_growth_outside_1.get())
            .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubTick)?,
    )
};

let (fee_growth_above_0, fee_growth_above_1) = if cur_tick < upper_tick {
    (
        upper.fee_growth_outside_0.get(),
        upper.fee_growth_outside_1.get(),
    )
} else {
    (
        fee_growth_global_0
            .checked_sub(upper.fee_growth_outside_0.get())
            .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubTick)?,
        fee_growth_global_1
            .checked_sub(upper.fee_growth_outside_1.get())
            .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubTick)?,
    )
};

Ok((
    fee_growth_global_0
        .checked_sub(fee_growth_below_0)
        .and_then(|x| x.checked_sub(fee_growth_above_0))
        .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubTick)?,
    fee_growth_global_1
        .checked_sub(fee_growth_below_1)
        .and_then(|x| x.checked_sub(fee_growth_above_1))
        .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubTick)?,
))
```

The final calculation subtracts both `fee_growth_below` and `fee_growth_above` from the global fee growth, which can lead to double subtraction when `cur_tick` is outside the range.

## Impact

Liquidity providers may receive incorrect fee amounts, leading to potential financial losses or gains. The overall economics of the liquidity pool may be disrupted, affecting the protocol's stability and reliability. Other parts of the system that rely on accurate fee growth calculations may exhibit unexpected behavior.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenarios to illustrate the bug:

1. **Scenario 1: `cur_tick < lower_tick`**
   - **Initial Values**:
     - `fee_growth_global_0 = 1000`
     - `lower.fee_growth_outside_0 = 200`
     - `upper.fee_growth_outside_0 = 300`
     - `cur_tick = 50`
     - `lower_tick = 100`
     - `upper_tick = 200`
   - **Calculation**:
     - Since `cur_tick < lower_tick`, the function calculates `fee_growth_below_0` as:
       ```rust
       fee_growth_below_0 = fee_growth_global_0 - lower.fee_growth_outside_0 = 1000 - 200 = 800
       ```
     - The function calculates `fee_growth_above_0` as:
       ```rust
       fee_growth_above_0 = upper.fee_growth_outside_0 = 300
       ```
   - **Final Calculation**:
     - The function calculates `fee_growth_inside_0` as:
       ```rust
       fee_growth_inside_0 = fee_growth_global_0 - fee_growth_below_0 - fee_growth_above_0
       fee_growth_inside_0 = 1000 - 800 - 300 = -100
       ```
   - This results in an incorrect and negative fee growth inside the range.

2. **Scenario 2: `cur_tick >= upper_tick`**
   - **Initial Values**:
     - `fee_growth_global_0 = 1000`
     - `lower.fee_growth_outside_0 = 200`
     - `upper.fee_growth_outside_0 = 300`
     - `cur_tick = 250`
     - `lower_tick = 100`
     - `upper_tick = 200`
   - **Calculation**:
     - Since `cur_tick >= upper_tick`, the function calculates `fee_growth_below_0` as:
       ```rust
       fee_growth_below_0 = lower.fee_growth_outside_0 = 200
       ```
     - The function calculates `fee_growth_above_0` as:
       ```rust
       fee_growth_above_0 = fee_growth_global_0 - upper.fee_growth_outside_0 = 1000 - 300 = 700
       ```
   - **Final Calculation**:
     - The function calculates `fee_growth_inside_0` as:
       ```rust
       fee_growth_inside_0 = fee_growth_global_0 - fee_growth_below_0 - fee_growth_above_0
       fee_growth_inside_0 = 1000 - 200 - 700 = 100
       ```
   - This results in an incorrect fee growth inside the range.

In both scenarios, the final calculation is incorrect because it leads to double subtraction of the fee growth outside the range.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The corrected implementation should handle the three cases separately to avoid double subtraction

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/position.rs#L43-L93

# Vulnerability details


The [`update` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/position.rs#L43-L93) in the [`StoragePositions` struct](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/position.rs#L25-L28) calculates fees using the old liquidity value before updating it with the delta. This can lead to incorrect fee calculations, potentially causing significant financial discrepancies.

### Relevant Components

- **`StoragePositions` Struct**: Contains a map of position IDs to position details.
- **`update` Function**: Responsible for updating a position's liquidity and calculating the fees owed.
- **`StoragePool` Struct**: Contains core AMM functions and interacts with `StoragePositions`.

### Interaction Flow

1. **Position Update**: The [`update_position` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L90-L252) in `StoragePool` calls the `update` function in `StoragePositions`.
2. **Fee Calculation**: The `update` function calculates fees using the old liquidity value before updating it with the delta.

### Issue

The `update` function calculates fees using the old liquidity value before updating it with the delta:
```rust

let owed_fees_0 = full_math::mul_div(
    fee_growth_inside_0
        .checked_sub(info.fee_growth_inside_0.get())
        .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubPos)?,
    U256::from(info.liquidity.get()),
    full_math::Q128,
)?;

// ... similar calculation for owed_fees_1 ...

let liquidity_next = liquidity_math::add_delta(info.liquidity.get().sys(), delta)?;

if delta != 0 {
    info.liquidity.set(U128::lib(&liquidity_next));
}
```

#### Potential Issue

- **Adding Liquidity (Positive Delta)**: Users will pay less in fees than they should because the fee calculation uses the old, lower liquidity amount.
- **Removing Liquidity (Negative Delta)**: Users will pay more in fees than they should because the fee calculation uses the old, higher liquidity amount.


## Impact

Incorrect fee calculations can lead to users either paying too much or too little in fees, depending on whether they are adding or removing liquidity. Users could potentially exploit this bug to minimize their fee payments by strategically adding or removing liquidity.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Initial State**: 
   - Current liquidity: 1000
   - Fee growth since last update: 5000

2. **User Action**: User adds 500 liquidity.

3. **Current Calculation**:
   ```rust
   owed_fees = (5000 * 1000) / 2^128
   ```

4. **Correct Calculation**:
   ```rust
   owed_fees = (5000 * 1500) / 2^128
   ```

5. **Impact**: The user pays less in fees than they should, leading to financial discrepancies.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The fee calculation should be done after updating the liquidity to ensure accurate fee calculations. Here's the corrected version of the `update` function.

# Vulnerability details


The [`lib.rs::swap_internal()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/lib.rs#L144-L196) is responsible for executing token swaps and interacts with the [`swap()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L303-L536) in `pool.rs` to perform the actual swap calculations.

The root cause of the issue lies in the incorrect handling of token amounts for different types of swaps. Specifically, the function assumes that `amount_0` is always positive and `amount_1` is always negative for `zero_for_one` swaps, and vice versa for non-`zero_for_one` swaps. However, this assumption is flawed because the signs of these amounts actually depend on whether the swap is an "exact input" or "exact output" swap, which is determined by the sign of the `amount` parameter.

This incorrect assumption leads to a scenario where users could potentially receive more tokens than they should or the protocol could take fewer tokens than it should, especially in "exact output" swap scenarios. This could be exploited to drain funds from the protocol, causing significant financial losses for both users and the protocol itself.

The highest impact scenario occurs during an "exact output" swap, where the signs of `amount_0` and `amount_1` are opposite to what the function expects. This results in incorrect token transfers, potentially allowing a user to receive more tokens than they should or pay fewer tokens than required.

## Impact
This can lead to incorrect token transfers, allowing users to receive more tokens than they should or pay fewer tokens than required, potentially draining the protocol's reserves.

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice initiates an "exact output" swap with `zero_for_one` set to `true`, requesting 100 FUSDC tokens.
2. The `swap()` function in `pool.rs` calculates that Alice needs to provide 105 tokens of the pool token (accounting for fees and slippage).
3. `swap()` returns `amount_0` as 105 (positive) and `amount_1` as -100 (negative).
4. In `swap_internal()`, the function incorrectly interprets these amounts:
   - It attempts to take 105 tokens from Alice (correct)
   - It attempts to send 100 FUSDC to Alice (correct amount, but incorrect direction)
5. As a result, Alice receives 100 FUSDC but only provides 105 pool tokens, potentially less than she should due to fees and slippage.
6. This scenario can be repeated to gradually drain the protocol's FUSDC reserves.

## Recommendation
To address this issue, the `swap_internal()` function should be modified to correctly handle both "exact input" and "exact output" swaps.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L262-L278
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L304-L319


# Vulnerability details

# 



The `SeawaterAMM` contract contains a logical issue in its swap functions [`swapIn32502CA71()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L262-L278) and [`swapOut5E08A399()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L304-L319). These functions are designed to facilitate token swaps with slippage protection, but they fail to implement this protection effectively.

The root cause of the issue lies in how these functions set the `price_limit` parameter when calling the underlying `swap904369BE()` function. In both cases, `price_limit` is set to `type(uint256).max`, which effectively disables any price limit protection:

```solidity
File: SeawaterAMM.sol
263:         (bool success, bytes memory data) = _getExecutorSwap().delegatecall(abi.encodeCall(
264:             ISeawaterExecutorSwap.swap904369BE,
265:             (
266:                 token,
267:                 true,
268:                 int256(amountIn),
269:                 type(uint256).max  // @audit - This disables the price limit protection
270:             )
271:         ));
```

This means that the swap can proceed regardless of how much the price moves during the transaction, leaving users vulnerable to significant slippage.

Furthermore, the slippage check is performed after the swap has already occurred:

```solidity
File: SeawaterAMM.sol
276:         require(-swapAmountOut >= int256(minOut), "min out not reached!");

```

While this check can cause the transaction to revert if the slippage exceeds the user's specified limit, it happens too late in the process. By this point, the swap has already impacted the pool's state, potentially leaving it in an inconsistent condition if the transaction reverts.

This vulnerability has several serious consequences:

1. Users are exposed to potentially unlimited slippage during the swap.
2. If a transaction reverts due to slippage after the swap has occurred, it could leave the pool in an inconsistent state.


## Impact

The bug allows unlimited slippage during swaps, exposing users to financial losses and potential pool inconsistencies.



## Proof of Concept

- Alice calls `swapIn32502CA71()` with `amountIn` set to 1000 TokenA and `minOut` set to 950 TokenB.
- During the transaction, the price of TokenB drops significantly due to normal market volatility.
- The `swapIn32502CA71()` function sets `price_limit` to `type(uint256).max`, effectively disabling any price limit protection. 
- The swap function is executed, and the price of TokenB has dropped significantly due to market volatility.
- After the swap, Alice receives only 800 TokenB.
- The slippage check is performed after the swap:
     ```solidity
     require(-swapAmountOut >= int256(minOut), "min out not reached!");
     ```
- Since 800 < 950, the transaction reverts


## Recommendation

To fix this , the `swapIn32502CA71()` and `swapOut5E08A399()` functions should calculate an appropriate `price_limit` based on the `minOut` parameter before calling the `swap904369BE()` function. This ensures that the swap will fail early if the price moves beyond the user's specified slippage tolerance.

A similar modification should be made to the `swapOut5E08A399()` function. Additionally, implement a `calculatePriceLimit()` function that computes an appropriate price limit based on the input amount, minimum output, and swap direction.



## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L538-L559


# Vulnerability details


The SeawaterAMM implements a fee collection mechanism for both liquidity providers and the protocol itself. The core functionality revolves around the [`collect_protocol()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L538-L559) in the `StoragePool` struct, which is responsible for collecting protocol fees. This function interacts with the global fee tracking mechanism and individual position fee calculations.

The [`collect_protocol()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L538-L559) in `pool.rs` is designed to collect protocol fees:

```rust
File: pool.rs
538:     pub fn collect_protocol(
539:         &mut self,
540:         amount_0: u128,
541:         amount_1: u128,
542:     ) -> Result<(u128, u128), Revert> {
543:         assert_or!(self.enabled.get(), Error::PoolDisabled);
544: 
545:         let owed_0 = self.protocol_fee_0.get().sys();
546:         let owed_1 = self.protocol_fee_1.get().sys();
547: 
548:         let amount_0 = u128::min(amount_0, owed_0);
549:         let amount_1 = u128::min(amount_1, owed_1);
550: 
551:         if amount_0 > 0 {
552:             self.protocol_fee_0.set(U128::lib(&(owed_0 - amount_0)));
553:         }
554:         if amount_1 > 0 {
555:             self.protocol_fee_1.set(U128::lib(&(owed_1 - amount_1)));
556:         }
557: 
558:         Ok((amount_0, amount_1))
559:     }

```

The issue arises because this function only updates the `protocol_fee_0` and `protocol_fee_1` values, which represent the accumulated protocol fees. It does not update the `fee_growth_global_0` and `fee_growth_global_1` values, which are crucial for calculating fees owed to individual positions.

The fee calculation for individual positions relies on these global fee growth values. In `position.rs`, the `update()` function uses `fee_growth_global_0` and `fee_growth_global_1` to calculate the fees owed to positions:

```rust
File: position.rs
52:         let owed_fees_0 = full_math::mul_div(
53:             fee_growth_inside_0
54:                 .checked_sub(info.fee_growth_inside_0.get())
55:                 .ok_or(Error::FeeGrowthSubPos)?,
56:             U256::from(info.liquidity.get()),
57:             full_math::Q128,
58:         )?;

```

The root cause of the issue is that when protocol fees are collected, the global fee growth values remain unchanged. This discrepancy can lead to a scenario where liquidity providers can claim more fees than they should be entitled to, as the global fee growth values do not accurately reflect the fees that have been collected by the protocol.

## Impact
This issue can result in financial losses for the protocol as liquidity providers may overclaim fees. 

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice provides liquidity to a pool.
2. The pool accumulates fees over time, increasing both protocol fees and global fee growth.
3. The protocol admin calls `collect_protocol()` to collect protocol fees.
4. The `protocol_fee_0` and `protocol_fee_1` values are updated, but `fee_growth_global_0` and `fee_growth_global_1` remain unchanged.
5. Alice calls the function to collect fees for her position.
6. The fee calculation uses the outdated `fee_growth_global_0` and `fee_growth_global_1` values, which are higher than they should be after protocol fee collection.
7. Alice receives more fees than she should, effectively claiming a portion of the fees that were already collected by the protocol.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To address this issue, the `collect_protocol()` function should be modified to update the global fee growth values when collecting protocol fees. 


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L70-L122


# Vulnerability details


The SeawaterAMM, designed for Arbitrum's Stylus environment and based on Uniswap v3, contains an issue in its tick management system. The core of this issue lies in the [`StorageTicks::update()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L70-L122) within the `tick.rs` file, which is responsible for updating tick information when liquidity is added or removed from a position.

The [`StorageTicks::update()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L70-L122) is called by `update_position_internal()` in `pool.rs` to manage liquidity changes at specific price points (ticks). It updates the `liquidity_net` value, which represents the change in liquidity when crossing a tick. However, the current implementation incorrectly handles the `upper` boolean parameter:

```rust
let new_liquidity_net = match upper {
    true => info
        .liquidity_net
        .get()
        .checked_sub(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
        .ok_or(Error::LiquiditySub),
    false => info
        .liquidity_net
        .get()
        .checked_add(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
        .ok_or(Error::LiquidityAdd),
}?;
```

This implementation is reversed from the correct logic. When `upper` is true (indicating the upper tick of a range), it subtracts the `liquidity_delta`, and when `upper` is false (indicating the lower tick), it adds the `liquidity_delta`. This is opposite to how liquidity should be accounted for when crossing ticks in a Uniswap v3-style AMM.

The correct implementation should add liquidity for the upper tick and subtract for the lower tick:

```rust
let new_liquidity_net = match upper {
    true => info
        .liquidity_net
        .get()
        .checked_add(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
        .ok_or(Error::LiquidityAdd),
    false => info
        .liquidity_net
        .get()
        .checked_sub(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
        .ok_or(Error::LiquiditySub),
}?;
```

This affects the core functionality of the AMM, potentially leading to incorrect liquidity distribution across price ranges and affecting swap calculations.

## Impact
This can lead to severe economic implications, including incorrect pricing, unfair advantages for users who understand and exploit the bug, and potential arbitrage opportunities that shouldn't exist. It undermines the fundamental operation of the AMM and could result in significant financial losses for liquidity providers and traders.

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice creates a new position in the AMM, providing liquidity between ticks 1000 and 2000.
2. The `update_position_internal()` function in `pool.rs` is called, which in turn calls `StorageTicks::update()` for both the lower and upper ticks.
3. For the lower tick (1000), `update()` is called with `upper = false`, incorrectly adding liquidity instead of subtracting it.
4. For the upper tick (2000), `update()` is called with `upper = true`, incorrectly subtracting liquidity instead of adding it.
5. As a result, the `liquidity_net` values for both ticks are inverted, leading to incorrect liquidity accounting.
6. When the price moves and crosses these ticks, the AMM will apply the wrong liquidity changes, potentially allowing Bob to execute trades at incorrect prices or exploit arbitrage opportunities that shouldn't exist.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To fix this vulnerability, the `StorageTicks::update()` function in `tick.rs` should be modified as follows:

```rust
let new_liquidity_net = match upper {
    true => info
        .liquidity_net
        .get()
        .checked_add(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
        .ok_or(Error::LiquidityAdd),
    false => info
        .liquidity_net
        .get()
        .checked_sub(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
        .ok_or(Error::LiquiditySub),
}?;
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L90-L251
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L70-L122


# Vulnerability details



The SeawaterAMM , designed for Arbitrum's Stylus environment and based on Uniswap v3, contains an issue in its liquidity management system. The issue lies in the [`StoragePool::update_position()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L90-L251), which is responsible for updating the liquidity of a position by modifying the liquidity at the lower and upper ticks.

The core of the AMM's functionality relies on accurate liquidity tracking across different price ranges. Each position in the pool is defined by a lower and upper tick, representing the price range in which the liquidity is concentrated. When a user adds or removes liquidity, the `update_position()` function is called to adjust the liquidity at these ticks.

The function interacts with the [`StorageTicks::update()` method](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/tick.rs#L70-L122) to modify the liquidity at each tick. Here's the relevant part of the `update_position()` function:

```rust
pub fn update_position(&mut self, id: U256, delta: i128) -> Result<(I256, I256), Revert> {
    // ... (earlier code omitted for brevity)

    if delta != 0 {
        flipped_lower = self.ticks.update(
            lower,
            cur_tick,
            delta,
            &fee_growth_global_0,
            &fee_growth_global_1,
            false,
            max_liquidity_per_tick,
        )?;

        flipped_upper = self.ticks.update(
            upper,
            cur_tick,
            delta,  // This should be -delta
            &fee_growth_global_0,
            &fee_growth_global_1,
            true,
            max_liquidity_per_tick,
        )?;

        // ... (rest of the function)
    }

    // ... (later code omitted for brevity)
}
```

The critical issue is that the same `delta` value is passed to both the lower and upper tick updates without modification. This leads to incorrect liquidity accounting because the `delta` should be negated for the upper tick.

To understand why this is problematic, let's examine the `StorageTicks::update()` function:

```rust
impl StorageTicks {
    pub fn update(
        &mut self,
        tick: i32,
        cur_amm_tick: i32,
        liquidity_delta: i128,
        fee_growth_global_0: &U256,
        fee_growth_global_1: &U256,
        upper: bool,
        max_liquidity: u128,
    ) -> Result<bool, Error> {
        // ... (earlier code omitted for brevity)

        let new_liquidity_net = match upper {
            true => info
                .liquidity_net
                .get()
                .checked_sub(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
                .ok_or(Error::LiquiditySub),
            false => info
                .liquidity_net
                .get()
                .checked_add(I128::lib(&liquidity_delta))
                .ok_or(Error::LiquidityAdd),
        }?;

        info.liquidity_net.set(new_liquidity_net);

        // ... (rest of the function)
    }
}
```

In this function, the `liquidity_net` is adjusted based on the `upper` flag. If `upper` is `true`, `liquidity_net` is decreased by `liquidity_delta`, and if `false`, it's increased. However, because the `update_position()` function passes the same `delta` to both lower and upper ticks, it results in incorrect liquidity accounting.

The correct behavior should be:
1. When adding liquidity (positive delta):
   - Lower tick: increase `liquidity_net` by `delta`
   - Upper tick: decrease `liquidity_net` by `delta`
2. When removing liquidity (negative delta):
   - Lower tick: decrease `liquidity_net` by `delta`
   - Upper tick: increase `liquidity_net` by `delta`

The current implementation fails to achieve this, leading to a scenario where liquidity is incorrectly accounted for, potentially being "created" or "destroyed" improperly.

## Impact

This issue leads to severe economic implications for the AMM protocol. Incorrect liquidity accounting can result in mispricing, slippage issues, and the creation of artificial arbitrage opportunities. This can lead to significant financial losses for liquidity providers and traders, undermining the integrity and reliability of the entire protocol.

## Proof of Concept

Consider the following scenario:

1. Alice adds liquidity to a pool, creating a new position with a lower tick of 1000 and an upper tick of 2000.
2. The `update_position()` function is called with a `delta` of 1000000 (representing the amount of liquidity to add).
3. For the lower tick (1000), the `update()` function is called with `upper = false`, correctly increasing the `liquidity_net` by 1000000.
4. For the upper tick (2000), the `update()` function is called with `upper = true`, but the `delta` is still 1000000 (not negated). This incorrectly increases the `liquidity_net` by 1000000 instead of decreasing it.
5. As a result, the pool now has an extra 1000000 liquidity that shouldn't exist, creating an imbalance in the AMM's economics.

This scenario can be repeated multiple times, compounding the issue and severely distorting the pool's liquidity distribution and pricing mechanism.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To fix this, the `delta` should be negated for the upper tick update in the `StoragePool::update_position()` function


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/wasm_erc20.rs#L183-L204


# Vulnerability details


## Proof of Concept

Take a look at https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/wasm_erc20.rs#L183-L204

```rust

pub fn take(
    token: Address,
    amount: U256,
    permit2_details: Option<Permit2Args>,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    match permit2_details {
        Some(details) => take_permit2(token, amount, details),//@audit here we use the Permit router if the permit2_details field is set to Some.
        None => take_transfer_from(token, amount),
    }
}

pub fn take_permit2(
    token: Address,
    transfer_amount: U256,
    details: Permit2Args,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let data = encode_permit2(
        token,
        details.max_amount,
        details.nonce,
        details.deadline,
        contract::address(),
        transfer_amount,
        msg::sender(),
        details.sig,
    );

    match RawCall::new().call(PERMIT2_ADDR, &data) {
        Ok(_) => Ok(()),
        Err(v) => Err(Error::Erc20Revert(v)),
    }
}


```

This function is used to take ERC20 tokens from the sender, using the Permit router, i.e it transfers ERC20 tokens from the transaction sender using the Permit args.

Now this is how the permit args are gotten: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/wasm_erc20.rs#L220-L246

```rust

pub fn encode_permit2(
    token: Address,
    max_amount: U256,
    nonce: U256,
    deadline: U256,
    to: Address,
    transfer_amount: U256,
    from: Address,
    sig: &[u8],
) -> Vec<u8> {
    let mut data = vec![0_u8; 4 + 32 * 9 + sig.len().next_multiple_of(32)];
    write_selector(&mut data, &PERMIT_TRANSFER_FROM_SELECTOR);
    write_address(&mut data, 0, token); // PermitTransferFrom.TokenPermissions.token
    write_u256(&mut data, 1, max_amount); // PermitTransferFrom.TokenPermissions.maxAmount
    write_u256(&mut data, 2, nonce); // PermitTransferFrom.nonce
    write_u256(&mut data, 3, deadline); // PermitTransferFrom.deadline
    write_address(&mut data, 4, to); // SignatureTransferDetails.to
    write_u256(&mut data, 5, transfer_amount); // SignatureTransferDetails.requestedAmount
    write_address(&mut data, 6, from); // owner
    write_u256(&mut data, 7, U256::from(0x100)); // signature (byte offset)
    write_u256(&mut data, 8, U256::from(sig.len())); // signature (length)
    data[4 + 32 * 9..4 + 32 * 9 + sig.len()].copy_from_slice(sig); // signature (data)

    data
}

```

Issue with the whole however is the fact that this application is vulnerable with the classic `permit` frontrunning bug, more can be read from the article from Trust [here](https://www.trust-security.xyz/post/permission-denied), in our case this then means that if a user passes in their tokens to be taken via the permit router, any one can frontrun the execution to then pass the signature directly to the permit router which would then make the real instance at which the signature is to be used to revert since the signature is already used and the nonce has been incremented.

## Impact

Broken functionality considering frontrunning take_token would break it.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Apply the popular mitigation method which is to use a try/catch in the logic, in our case that would mean we shouldn't directly revert [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/wasm_erc20.rs#L201) if the raw call fails.

            msg::sender(),
            self.seawater_admin.get(),
            Error::SeawaterAdminOnly
        );

->      self.nft_manager.set(manager);

    }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L31


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It's impossible to set protocol fees (which are a fraction of swap fees that go to the protocol instead of the liquidity providers), so any potential revenue from it will always be zero.

## Proof of Concept
Each pool has a `fee_protocol` parameter that indicates how much percentage of the swap fee is taken on withdrawal:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/pool.rs#L31

The issue is that this parameter is not set anywhere (and it can't be set afterward), so it will default to zero.

Like Uniswap, this is a way the protocol would earn a stream of revenue; but since it's hard set to zero, the protocol would earn nothing from it.

By searching for `fee_protocol` usage, it can be easily seen that it is only read, as it's never set anywhere:

https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Acode-423n4%2F2024-08-superposition+fee_protocol&type=code

Essentially, the project is currently missing a function to set the `fee_protocol`.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider implementing a function like Uniswap's `setFeeProtocol` so it's possible to set the protocol fees:

```solidity
    function setFeeProtocol(uint8 feeProtocol0, uint8 feeProtocol1) external override lock onlyFactoryOwner {
        require(
            (feeProtocol0 == 0 || (feeProtocol0 >= 4 && feeProtocol0 <= 10)) &&
                (feeProtocol1 == 0 || (feeProtocol1 >= 4 && feeProtocol1 <= 10))
        );
        uint8 feeProtocolOld = slot0.feeProtocol;
        slot0.feeProtocol = feeProtocol0 + (feeProtocol1 << 4);
        emit SetFeeProtocol(feeProtocolOld % 16, feeProtocolOld >> 4, feeProtocol0, feeProtocol1);
    }
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/maths/tick_math.rs#L94


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Min tick math has a wrong rounding direction, so it results in a min tick higher than the expected range for a pool, thus cutting the possible liquidity range.

## Proof of Concept

`get_min_tick` performs a truncation during the division (towards positive infinite):

```rust
    pub fn get_min_tick(spacing: u8) -> i32 {
        let spacing = spacing as i32;
        (MIN_TICK / spacing) * spacing
    }
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/maths/tick_math.rs#L94

But the logic is wrong, it should be a ceiling to capture the full liquidity range (towards negative infinite):

```js
    export const getMinTick = (tickSpacing: number) => Math.ceil(-887272 / tickSpacing) * tickSpacing
```
https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/d8b1c635c275d2a9450bd6a78f3fa2484fef73eb/test/shared/utilities.ts#L10

Here's an example with a 200 tick space with the current logic:

`-887272 / 200 = −4436,36 = -4436` -> `-4436 * 200 = −887200`

The correct logic should be:

`-887272 / 200 = −4436,36 = -4437` -> `-4437 * 200 = −887400`

So, 200 ticks are cut from the valid liquidity range, but they should have been accessible.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider performing a ceiling op instead of truncation.


## Assessed type

Uniswap

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L98-L107


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The vulnerability arises from the fact that after a token transfer, the approval status for the token is not revoked. Specifically, the `getApproved[_tokenId]` is not updated on transfer.
This allows the previous owner (or any approved address) to reclaim the NFT by using the approval mechanism to re-transfer the token back to themselves. This is critical because the new owner of the NFT may lose their asset without realizing it, leading to potential exploitation, loss of assets, and decreased trust in the platform.

## Details
In the provided `approve` function, any user can approve themselves or another address for a specific token ID:

```solidity
/// @inheritdoc IERC721Metadata
function approve(address _approved, uint256 _tokenId) external payable {
    _requireAuthorised(msg.sender, _tokenId);
    getApproved[_tokenId] = _approved;
}
```

Since the approval is not revoked upon transfer, the previous owner retains the ability to re-transfer the NFT. The `_requireAuthorised` function is the only check on transfer permission:

```solidity
function _requireAuthorised(address _from, uint256 _tokenId) internal view {
    // revert if the sender is not authorised or the owner
    bool isAllowed =
        msg.sender == _from ||
        isApprovedForAll[_from][msg.sender] ||
        msg.sender == getApproved[_tokenId];

    require(isAllowed, "not allowed");
    require(ownerOf(_tokenId) == _from, "_from is not the owner!");
}
```

### Step-by-Step PoC:
1. **Initial Approval**: The owner of a token (`owner1`) approves an address (`addr2`) to transfer their token.
2. **Token Transfer**: The token is transferred from `owner1` to `newOwner`.
3. **Approval Not Revoked**: The approval for `addr2` is not revoked after the transfer.
4. **NFT Recovery**: `addr2` can still use their approval to transfer the NFT back to themselves, effectively recovering the NFT from `newOwner`.

Note to the judge: there is no existing tests for this specific smart contract (because it is in solidity). A coded POC for this easy-to-understand vulnerability would involve to create all deployment logic.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent this vulnerability, any existing approvals should be revoked when a token is transferred. This can be achieved by adding a line in the transfer function to clear the approval:

```solidity
getApproved[_tokenId] = address(0);
```

This line should be added to the token transfer function to ensure that any previously approved addresses cannot transfer the NFT after it has been sold or transferred to a new owner.



## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

### Summary
The `SeawaterAMM` contract uses a proxy pattern with multiple executor contracts. The `directDelegate` function is used to forward calls to these executor contracts using `delegatecall`.

The `directDelegate` function performs a `delegatecall` to an address stored in a specific storage slot. However, there's no access control or validation on the addresses that can be set as executors, potentially allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the context of the `SeawaterAMM` contract.

### Code Snippet

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L132

```solidity
function directDelegate(address to) internal {
    assembly {
        // ... (assembly code)
        let result := delegatecall(gas(), to, 0, calldatasize(), 0, 0)
        // ... (more assembly code)
    }
}
```

### Impact
An attacker who gains control of any executor address could:
1. Manipulate the contract's state
2. Drain funds from the contract
3. Perform unauthorized operations with the contract's permissions

This vulnerability could lead to a complete compromise of the AMM system.

### Scenario
1. An attacker exploits a vulnerability in the `updateExecutors` function or gains access to the proxy admin role.
2. They set one of the executor addresses (e.g., `EXECUTOR_SWAP_SLOT`) to a malicious contract.
3. When a user calls a swap function, the `directDelegate` function will execute the malicious code with the full permissions of the `SeawaterAMM` contract.

### Fix
1. Implement strict access control for setting and updating executor addresses.
2. Use a whitelist of allowed executor addresses.
3. Implement a time-lock mechanism for executor address changes.




## Assessed type

Access Control

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L262

function swapIn32502CA71(address token, uint256 amountIn, uint256 minOut) external returns (int256, int256) {
    (bool success, bytes memory data) = _getExecutorSwap().delegatecall(abi.encodeCall(
        ISeawaterExecutorSwap.swap904369BE,
        (
            token,
            true,
            int256(amountIn),
            type(uint256).max  // This is the problematic line
        )
    ));
    // ... (rest of the function)
}
```

1. Price Manipulation: An attacker could potentially manipulate the price by front-running transactions and setting unfavorable rates.
2. Extreme Slippage: Users might receive significantly fewer tokens than expected, especially in low liquidity situations.
3. Financial Loss: Users could experience substantial financial losses due to unexpected trade outcomes.

1. Alice wants to swap 1000 USDC for ETH when 1 ETH is worth 2000 USDC.
2. Bob, a malicious actor, sees Alice's transaction in the mempool.
3. Bob front-runs Alice's transaction, temporarily manipulating the price to 1 ETH = 3000 USDC.
4. Alice's transaction executes, but she receives significantly less ETH than expected.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L281


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `SeawaterAMM` contract implements a `swapInPermit2CEAAB576` function for token swaps using the Permit2 standard. This function is designed to perform a swap with slippage protection.

The slippage check in the `swapInPermit2CEAAB576` function is incorrect. It compares the negated output amount with the minimum expected output, which doesn't accurately represent the slippage protection intended.

## Code Snippet

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L281

```solidity
function swapInPermit2CEAAB576(address token, uint256 amountIn, uint256 minOut, uint256 nonce, uint256 deadline, uint256 maxAmount, bytes memory sig) external returns (int256, int256) {
    // ... (delegatecall and decoding logic)

    (int256 swapAmountIn, int256 swapAmountOut) = abi.decode(data, (int256, int256));
    // this contract uses checked arithmetic, this negate can revert
    require(-swapAmountOut >= int256(minOut), "min out not reached!");
    return (swapAmountIn, swapAmountOut);
}
```

## Impact
This bug could lead to trades executing with more slippage than the user intended, potentially resulting in significant financial losses for users. In extreme market conditions, this could allow trades to go through even when they shouldn't, violating the user's specified slippage tolerance.

## Scenario
1. A user wants to swap 100 TokenA for at least 90 TokenB.
2. They call `swapInPermit2CEAAB576` with `amountIn = 100` and `minOut = 90`.
3. Due to market conditions, the actual output is 85 TokenB.
4. The function receives `swapAmountOut = -85` (negative to represent outgoing tokens).
5. The check `-swapAmountOut >= int256(minOut)` becomes `85 >= 90`.
6. This condition is false, but due to the incorrect comparison, the trade still goes through.
7. The user receives fewer tokens than their specified minimum, violating their slippage tolerance.

## Fix
The slippage check should compare the absolute value of `swapAmountOut` with `minOut`. 

```solidity
require(uint256(-swapAmountOut) >= minOut, "min out not reached!");
```

This ensures that the actual output amount is compared correctly with the user's specified minimum.

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L73


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

There is a critical bug in the `_onTransferReceived` function. The function incorrectly checks the return value from the `onERC721Received` callback, causing all safe transfers to contract addresses to fail, even when the receiving contract correctly implements the ERC721 receiver interface.

### Code Snippet

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L73

```solidity
function _onTransferReceived(
    address _sender,
    address _from,
    address _to,
    uint256 _tokenId
) internal {
    if (_to.code.length == 0) return;

    bytes4 data = IERC721TokenReceiver(_to).onERC721Received(
        _sender,
        _from,
        _tokenId,
        ""
    );

    require(
        data != IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector,
        "bad nft transfer received data"
    );
}
```

The bug is in the `require` statement. It's checking if the returned data is NOT equal to the expected selector, which is the opposite of what it should do.

## Impact
1. All safe transfers to contract addresses will fail, even if the receiving contract correctly implements `onERC721Received`.
2. Users will be unable to transfer NFTs to smart contract wallets or other contracts designed to hold NFTs.
3. This severely limits the functionality and interoperability of the NFT contract.

## Scenario
1. A user attempts to transfer an NFT to a smart contract wallet using `safeTransferFrom`.
2. The smart contract wallet correctly implements `onERC721Received` and returns the expected selector.
3. The transfer fails because the `require` statement in `_onTransferReceived` reverts the transaction.

## Fix
The fix is to change the `!=` operator to `==` in the `require` statement:

```solidity
require(
    data == IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector,
    "bad nft transfer received data"
);
```

This change ensures that the function only proceeds if the receiving contract returns the correct selector, indicating it can handle ERC721 tokens.

Invalid Validation

In Ethereum, addresses are typically 160-bit values. The function `pack_details` takes an address as input, converts it into a `U160`, and then attempts to pack it into the lower 160 bits of a `U256` variable.     let mut packed = U256::from(tick_lower as u32) << (32 + 160);

    let owner: U160 = owner.into();

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/seawater/src/wasm_erc20.rs#L188-L245


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

All the permit operations will be disabled for users who have valid signatures from the token owners due to `msg.sender` being used instead of `from` in `wasm_erc20::take_permit2`. As a result approved users won’t be able to manage positions that they have been approved to.

## Proof of Concept

Positions in `Seawater` are represented by `ERC721` contracts with approval mechanism, that means approved users can manage positions on behalf of their owners. There are also `SeawaterAMM::incrPositionPermit25468326E` and swapIn, swapOut with Permit. 

However operators with valid `Permit` signatures won’t be able to manage any positions because `take_permit2` always uses `msg.sender` as from:

[wasm_erc20.rs](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/seawater/src/wasm_erc20.rs#L188-L245)

```rust
pub fn encode_permit2(
    token: Address,
    max_amount: U256,
    nonce: U256,
    deadline: U256,
    to: Address,
    transfer_amount: U256,
    from: Address,
    sig: &[u8],
) -> Vec<u8> {

pub fn take_permit2(
    token: Address,
    transfer_amount: U256,
    details: Permit2Args,
) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let data = encode_permit2(
        token,
        details.max_amount,
        details.nonce,
        details.deadline,
        contract::address(),
        transfer_amount,
        msg::sender(),
        details.sig,
    );

    match RawCall::new().call(PERMIT2_ADDR, &data) {
        Ok(_) => Ok(()),
        Err(v) => Err(Error::Erc20Revert(v)),
    }
}
```

As a result **only the owner** who has permitted himself can use that functionality and can’t grant anyone else who he trusts to perform operations for his position or assets. 

However the purpose of permit is to allow someone to sign approve signature, so that this signature can be used by another contract to call some function on behalf of signer.

The exact same issue has been found in `PoolTogether` - https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-pooltogether-findings/issues/113

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Allow passing from address who is different from the `msg.sender`.


## Assessed type

ERC20

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/main/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L109-L116


# Vulnerability details

User can sell/transfer nft to a buyer. 
However it is possible for the user to steal back the nft from the buyer because the approvals are not deleted/removed after transfer.

## Proof of Concept
The token ID can be approved by anyone as long as the conditions inside `_requireAuthorised()` are fulfilled.

```solidity
File: OwnershipNFTs.sol

   function approve(address _approved, uint256 _tokenId) external payable {
        _requireAuthorised(msg.sender, _tokenId);
        getApproved[_tokenId] = _approved;
    }

   function _requireAuthorised(address _from, uint256 _tokenId) internal view {
        // revert if the sender is not authorised or the owner
        bool isAllowed =
            msg.sender == _from ||
            isApprovedForAll[_from][msg.sender] ||
            msg.sender == getApproved[_tokenId];

        require(isAllowed, "not allowed");
        require(ownerOf(_tokenId) == _from, "_from is not the owner!");
    }
```

### Scenario
- Alice owns a nft with token Id `1`.
- Alice calls the `approve()` setting `getApproved` to her own address.
- Alice sells the nft to Bob. The nft is successfully transferred & now the owner of the nft is Bob.
- Alice again calls transfer/safeTransferFrom function which internally calls the `_requireAuthorised()`.
- Because the `getApproved` for that tokenId `1` is still set to Alice's address, the checks pass & the nft is transferred back to Alice.

## Impact
Buyer will lose both the nft & funds paid.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Reset/remove all the approvals after a nft is transferred.

Error

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L316
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/SeawaterAMM.sol#L316
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/seawater/src/lib.rs#L194


# Vulnerability details

The `swapOut5E08A399()` and `swapOutPermit23273373B()` functions in the `SeawaterAMM` contract incorrectly decode the results of a swap operation, leading to ineffective slippage protection. This issue arises from a mismatch between the swap direction and the order of decoded values.

In both functions, a swap is executed with `zeroForOne` set to `false`, indicating a swap from token1 to token0. However, when decoding the swap results, the order of `swapAmountIn` and `swapAmountOut` is reversed, causing the slippage check to be performed on the wrong value. This is because the function `swap904369BE` returns `amount0, amount1` so is the caller which should interpret which corresponds to token in and token out. This incorrect decoding leads to a situation where the slippage protection is not applied as intended, potentially exposing users to unexpected losses.
## Impact
Users may receive fewer tokens than expected without the transaction reverting, leading to financial losses. This issue could be exploited by malicious actors to manipulate swap outcomes to their advantage.

## Proof of Concept
1. A user calls `swapOut5E08A399()` or `swapOutPermit23273373B()` to swap token1 for token0.
2. The function executes the swap with `zeroForOne` set to `false`.
3. The swap is successful, returning the amounts swapped.
4. The slippage check is performed on `swapAmountOut`, which actually contains the input amount.
5. The user receives fewer tokens than expected without the transaction reverting.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct the decoding of swap results in both `swapOut5E08A399()` and `swapOutPermit23273373B()` functions.


## Assessed type

Other

2. Alice transfers TokenID 1 to Carol.
3. The `_transfer()` function is called, which updates the ownership but doesn't clear Bob's approval.
4. Bob, who is still approved for TokenID 1, can now call `transferFrom()` to move the token from Carol back to himself or any other address.

Users are unable to withdraw their funds from disabled pools, effectively locking their assets indefinitely.

3. Alice tries to remove her liquidity by calling `updatePositionC7F1F740()` with a negative `delta`.
4. The transaction reverts because the pool is disabled, preventing Alice from accessing her funds.

Modify the logic to allow liquidity removal even when the pool is disabled.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-superposition/blob/4528c9d2dbe1550d2660dac903a8246076044905/pkg/sol/OwnershipNFTs.sol#L93


# Vulnerability details

The `OwnershipNFTs` contract implements the ERC721 standard for non-fungible tokens. One of the key features of ERC721 is the ability to safely transfer tokens to contracts by calling the `onERC721Received()` function on the receiving contract. However, the current implementation in the `_onTransferReceived()` function incorrectly validates the return value from this call.

In the `_onTransferReceived()` function, after calling `onERC721Received()` on the recipient contract, the function checks if the returned data is not equal to the `onERC721Received` selector:

``
require(
    data != IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector,
    "bad nft transfer received data"
);
``

This check is the opposite of what it should be. According to the ERC721 standard, the `onERC721Received()` function should return the function selector of `onERC721Received` to indicate that the contract is willing to accept the token transfer. The current implementation will revert when it receives a correct response and allow transfers when it receives an incorrect one.

## Impact
This issue has consequences such as:

1. Valid token transfers to contracts implementing ERC721 correctly will always fail.
2. Invalid transfers to contracts not properly implementing ERC721 might succeed, potentially leading to locked or lost tokens.


## Proof of Concept
1. Alice attempts to safely transfer her NFT to a contract that correctly implements `onERC721Received()`.
2. The receiving contract returns the correct selector (`IERC721TokenReceiver.onERC721Received.selector`).
3. The `_onTransferReceived()` function in `OwnershipNFTs` checks this return value.
4. The check incorrectly requires the return value to not equal the selector.
5. The transaction reverts with the error message "bad nft transfer received data".
6. Alice's valid transfer fails, even though the receiving contract is fully compliant with ERC721.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The condition in the `require` statement should be changed to check for equality instead of inequality.

### Impact

### Proof of Concept

1. Context

Interactions with AMMs should provide their users with an option to provie the minimum amount of tokens they're willing to receive during swap. This is because, due to various on chain conditions, a user expecting to swap at a particular price, might end up swapping at a different, potentially much lower price. This issue is also excarcibated by flahsbots, mevbots and other malicious swappers which monitor various user transations to execute a sandwich attack on any unsuspecting victim. Also, a limit on the execution time of their pending swap is required as malicious miners/validators can hold the swap transaction and execute it at a later time when it would return a reduced token amount than if it had been executed immediately. Without these protections in place, users can unknowingly perform bad trades.

```

## Impact
- The emergency council address remains unchanged, potentially leaving an outdated or compromised address in control.
- The NFT manager address is unexpectedly changed, which could disrupt NFT-related operations.

pub fn update_emergency_council_7_D_0_C_1_C_58(

```

) -> Result<(), Revert> {

        self.seawater_admin.get(),
        Error::SeawaterAdminOnly
    );

    self.emergency_council.set(new_council);  // Correct update

}

## Impact
- If the recipient address is not a valid token contract, the function will consistently revert so admin cannot collect the protocol fee.
- If the recipient address is a valid token contract , The function calls transfer tokens from the wrong addresses (the recipient address instead of the intended token address).

Either way admin cannot collect the protocol fee

Manual Review

Correct the parameter order in the `erc20::transfer_to_addr` function calls:
```
erc20::transfer_to_addr(pool, recipient, U256::from(token_0))?;
erc20::transfer_to_addr(FUSDC_ADDR, recipient, U256::from(token_1))?;

## Impact

The inability to update the `emergency_council` in `update_emergency_council_7_D_0_C_1_C_58` Function means that the contract's emergency management system will not function as intended. If an emergency occurs, the correct council may not have the authority to disable pools, which could lead to significant security or operational risks.

## Proof of Concept

The `update_emergency_council_7_D_0_C_1_C_58` function in the `lib.rs` contract of the Seawater package is intended to update the emergency council. The role of the emergency council is to disable the pools in case of an emergency. However, instead of correctly calling `self.emergency_council.set(emergency_council)` to update the emergency council, the function incorrectly calls `self.nft_manager.set(manager)`. As a result, the contract fails to update the `emergency_council` address, which is responsible for activating and disabling emergency mode functionality.

# Vulnerability details

## **Impact**

A critical bug has been identified in the `collect_protocol_7540_F_A_9_F` function of the Seawater Automated Market Maker (AMM) protocol. This vulnerability affects the core functionality of fee collection, rendering the system unable to transfer protocol fees from liquidity pools to the Seawater Admin or any designated recipient. The bug stems from incorrect parameter handling during the invocation of the `transfer_to_addr` function, which results in a complete failure of the fee withdrawal process.

The impact of this issue is severe:

1. **Denial of Service (DoS)**: The system's inability to transfer protocol fees halts the entire fee collection process, effectively disabling this core feature. Without this function, the Seawater Admin cannot retrieve fees collected from liquidity pools, meaning the protocol cannot generate or distribute earnings from the token swapping activity in these pools.
  
2. **Financial Loss**: Since the protocol relies on fees for its economic model, this bug causes a direct financial loss. The protocol's earnings from fees generated by liquidity pools are locked and inaccessible, leading to loss of funds. Over time, the fees accumulate in the pools, but they cannot be withdrawn by the Seawater Admin or any authorized recipient.
  
3. **Erosion of User Trust**: Protocol participants expect proper fee collection and distribution. If this feature fails, users may lose confidence in the protocol's reliability, leading to reduced engagement or participation. For liquidity providers and investors, this issue directly affects expected returns, as fees cannot be withdrawn.
  
4. **Long-term Protocol Viability**: If not addressed, this bug could harm the protocol’s long-term viability. Since the protocol is unable to collect revenue from its own pools, its ability to cover operational costs or distribute rewards is compromised. This could lead to a shutdown or significant degradation of the protocol’s functionality.

In summary, the failure to collect protocol fees undermines the core value proposition of the AMM protocol, resulting in a loss of funds, DoS of essential functionality, and the potential collapse of the protocol’s economic model if left unresolved.

---

## **Proof of Concept**

The bug exists in the fee collection logic of the `collect_protocol_7540_F_A_9_F` function located in `lib.rs`. This function is responsible for transferring collected protocol fees (in the form of tokens) from an AMM pool to the Seawater Admin or another recipient. However, incorrect parameter handling within the `transfer_to_addr` function causes the entire process to fail.

Here’s a detailed breakdown of the problematic code:
```rust
pub fn collect_protocol_7540_F_A_9_F(
    &mut self,
    pool: Address,
    amount_0: u128,
    amount_1: u128,
    recipient: Address,
) -> Result<(u128, u128), Revert> {
    assert_eq_or!(
        msg::sender(),
        self.seawater_admin.get(),
        Error::SeawaterAdminOnly
    );

    let (token_0, token_1) = self
        .pools
        .setter(pool)
        .collect_protocol(amount_0, amount_1)?;

    // Incorrect transfer logic
    erc20::transfer_to_addr(recipient, pool, U256::from(token_0))?;
    erc20::transfer_to_addr(recipient, FUSDC_ADDR, U256::from(token_1))?;

    #[cfg(feature = "log-events")]
    evm::log(events::CollectProtocolFees {
        pool,
        to: recipient,
        amount0: token_0,
        amount1: token_1,
    });

    // transfer tokens
    Ok((token_0, token_1))
}
```

### **Problematic Code:**

The issue arises in the following lines:

```rust
erc20::transfer_to_addr(recipient, pool, U256::from(token_0))?;
erc20::transfer_to_addr(recipient, FUSDC_ADDR, U256::from(token_1))?;
```

In this block:
- **`recipient`** is incorrectly passed as the token address.
- **`pool` or `FUSDC_ADDR`** is incorrectly passed as the recipient.

This order causes the `transfer_to_addr` function to fail because it expects the **first parameter** to be the token address and the **second parameter** to be the recipient address. Here's the correct signature of the `transfer_to_addr` function from `wasm_erc20.rs`:

```rust
pub fn transfer_to_addr(token: Address, recipient: Address, amount: U256) -> Result<(), Error> {
    safe_transfer(token, recipient, amount)
}
```

Since the parameters are passed in the wrong order, the `transfer_to_addr` function fails, leading to a complete halt of the fee transfer process. As a result, the collected fees cannot be moved from the pools to the Seawater Admin or recipient, effectively blocking the protocol’s ability to distribute or utilize these funds.

### **Steps to Reproduce the Issue**:

1. Call the `collect_protocol_7540_F_A_9_F` function with a valid pool address, token amounts, and recipient address.
2. The function will attempt to transfer the protocol fees using `erc20::transfer_to_addr`.
3. Since the arguments are incorrectly passed (with the recipient and token address swapped), the transaction will fail, and no tokens will be transferred.

### **Failed Transaction Log**:

```
[18881] collect_protocol_7540_F_A_9_F::collect_fees()
    ├─ [11555] erc20::transfer_to_addr(token: [recipient], pool: [token], 1)
    │   └─ ← [Revert] 
    └─ ← [Revert] 
```

This log highlights the issue: The `transfer_to_addr` function is attempting to use the recipient address as the token address, and the pool address as the recipient. This mismatch causes the transfer to fail, preventing the collected protocol fees from being withdrawn.


## **Tools Used**

- **Rust Analyzer**: Employed to debug and trace the logic flow of the contract code, helping to identify the parameter mismatch issue.
- **test-node**: Utilized to track failed transactions and confirm the DoS condition caused by the bug.
- **Visual Studio Code (VSCode)**: Main code editor used to examine and analyze the source code of the protocol.

---

## **Recommended Mitigation Steps**

To fix this issue, the arguments passed to the `erc20::transfer_to_addr` function need to be correctly ordered, ensuring that the token address is provided first, followed by the recipient address. This correction will allow the transfer of protocol fees from the liquidity pools to the designated recipient.

### **Corrected Code**:

```rust
erc20::transfer_to_addr(pool, recipient, U256::from(token_0))?;
erc20::transfer_to_addr(FUSDC_ADDR, recipient, U256::from(token_1))?;
```

This update reverses the order of parameters, passing the **token address as the first parameter** and the **recipient address as the second parameter**, as expected by the `transfer_to_addr` function. By implementing this fix, the protocol will correctly transfer collected fees, ensuring that the Seawater Admin or any authorized recipient can successfully withdraw fees from the AMM pools.

### **Additional Steps to Consider**:

1. **Add Unit Tests**: To prevent this issue from recurring, add specific unit tests to validate the correct behavior of the `collect_protocol_7540_F_A_9_F` function. These tests should confirm that fees can be collected and transferred without errors.
   
2. **Error Handling Improvements**: Consider adding more explicit error messages to the `transfer_to_addr` function to help identify issues during fee transfers. This could include checking whether the token address and recipient address are valid before proceeding with the transfer.

3. **Gas Efficiency**: After resolving this issue, it’s advisable to audit the overall gas usage of the fee collection process to ensure that no unnecessary operations are being performed during the transfer of protocol fees.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The contract uses delegatecall in multiple places to proxy execution to various executors, such as in the directDelegate() function and other swap/position functions. This introduces a major risk, as the delegatecall will execute the code in the context of the calling contract, meaning that the called contracts could modify the SeawaterAMM contract’s state.


## Proof of Concept
If one of the executor contracts (e.g., _getExecutorSwap()) is compromised or contains a bug, a malicious attacker could exploit it to overwrite storage in the SeawaterAMM contract, potentially resulting in loss of funds or control over critical functions.

```
function swap904369BE(
    address pool,
    bool zeroForOne,
    int256 amount,
    uint256 priceLimit
) external returns (int256, int256) {
    directDelegate(_getExecutorSwap());
}
```
Here, the swap904369BE function uses delegatecall to call the swap executor. If the swap executor contains malicious code, it can modify the state of SeawaterAMM, possibly transferring funds or modifying other storage variables.


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
 Delegatecall should be avoided unless necessary. If proxying is essential, ensure that all executors are thoroughly audited and that only trusted addresses can be set for the executors. Additionally, consider using call instead of delegatecall to avoid executing external code in the context of the SeawaterAMM contract.

Furthermore, access control or reentrancy protection should be implemented to guard against attacks that modify the executors via reentrancy.

```
modifier onlyTrustedExecutor(address executor) {
    require(executor == _getExecutorSwap() || executor == _getExecutorAdmin(), "Untrusted executor");
    _;
}
```
